source.title: R3L: Relative Representations for Reinforcement Learning
source.authors: Antonio Pio Ricciardi; Valentino Maiorca; Luca Moschella; R. Marin; E. Rodolà

record.file_problem: none; full paper and appendix are present
record.tranche_reason: Tests relative-representation mapping and zero-shot stitching in visual reinforcement learning, a new setting, including outcomes across visual and task variations.
record.gate_note: The study reports relative-space similarity for aligned green/red CarRacing frames and stitching returns for CarRacing and Atari. Training curves and end-to-end returns are not included as rows because they do not directly measure cross-model representation alignment or stitching. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: Zero-shot stitching of encoders and controllers from independently trained visual-RL agents (different seeds, backgrounds, camera, tasks), via relative representations, tests V4 in a new setting. Caveat: the shared space is engineered, since every agent is trained end-to-end on relative (anchor-cosine) representations with EMA anchors and parallel anchor frames. It is not a test of whether natively trained models converge.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that relative representations with EMA-stabilized anchors give universal embeddings, allowing zero-shot stitching of independently trained encoders and controllers for unseen visual-task pairs and cutting training cost. They acknowledge weaker Atari stitching and controlled environments only.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts relative representations to online visual RL, using parallel samples from transformed observations or repeated action sequences and an exponential moving average of anchors to stabilize training. Uses PPO and tests encoder-controller stitching.
record.method_sensitivity: Stitching performance varies with environment and task/visual variation; slow-task CarRacing and Atari results are weaker or more variable. The study uses cosine similarity and does not compare it with other similarity measures.
record.problems: The experiments are restricted to controlled environments, and agents are trained from scratch. Figure 3 reports qualitative similarity without numeric values. Atari stitching has large standard deviations and a substantial drop relative to end-to-end R3L. The text does not provide an explicit alignment metric for the stitching tables; those rows measure task returns as evidence of successful component reuse.
record.rows_left_out: None. All reported CarRacing and Atari stitching cells were recorded, along with the qualitative aligned-frame similarity result.

untested.parts: Linear maps, layer stitching, mapping without paired data, cross-modal or cross-architecture mapping, and mapping between natively (absolute) trained models.
Different seeds are used, but there is no feature- or subspace-level analysis of native representations.
Cosine similarity only; no comparison of measures, anchors or input distributions.
No test of plateau or of causes of alignment.

missing.what: End-to-end R3L and absolute scores (no stitching). This is the reference needed to judge 'little loss' in stitching.
EMA ablation: alpha=0 (plain relative representations) trains poorly in online RL, so the alignment depends on the stabilization choice.

record.verdict_notes: The alignment is induced by design: agents are trained on relative representations with parallel anchors. The evidence therefore shows that interchangeability is achievable through relative representations, not that it arises natively. The absolute baseline is an unaligned naive stitch, so beating it is weak evidence on its own. S. multicolor rows are correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of model size or capability, or test of convergence as size and capability increase.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption representations.
Models do include different seeds, but the study does not test whether independently trained models learn shared features or subspaces in their native representations.
Tests relative representations and stitching in visual RL; does not test linear maps, layer stitching, relative representations across modalities, or mapping without paired data.
No interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are examined.
Uses cosine-based relative representations, but does not compare similarity measures, settings such as neighbour counts, or input distributions to test metric/data dependence.
Reports imperfect stitching performance in some settings, but does not test whether alignment plateaus or whether shared data/objectives rather than a common model of reality explain alignment.

rows.subject: two CarRacing encoders (names not stated)
rows.stage_stated: trained policies; training stage not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared pairwise cosine similarities of absolute and relative representations for frames from two encoders.

conditions.value: first ∼800 frames, aligned by replaying the same action sequence

rows.measure: Pairwise cosine similarity between latent spaces
rows.baseline: Absolute similarities described as consistently low, including on aligned frames.
rows.value: Strong similarity on the diagonal; similarities also occur off-diagonal, between semantically similar frames.
rows.note: The text describes the result qualitatively; the plotted values are not provided as numbers.
rows.check: Qualitative only, with no numbers. Section 4.1 says relative representations were computed from already-trained absolute models of different grass colors and seeds. The Fig. 3 caption says 'produced by the same model', which contradicts this. The subject should read: two CarRacing encoders, green vs red grass, different seeds.

relationships.condition: CarRacing, standard/scrambled/no-idle tasks, green/red/blue encoders, relative-representation-trained agents
relationships.reason: Stitched scores of 776–828 are near end-to-end R3L (797–874) and far above S. Abs (r2–r4, r6–r10, r12–r16, r18–r19).
relationships.display_finding: Stitched agents scored 776–828 versus 797–874 for end-to-end R3L, far above absolute stitching.

relationships.condition: CarRacing slow task and far-camera encoders
relationships.reason: Slow controller: 268–564, with SDs up to 440, vs E. R3L 624. Far encoder: 303–673 vs E. R3L 820 (r5, r11, r17, r20–r25).
relationships.display_finding: Slow-controller scores were 268–564 versus E. R3L's 624, with standard deviations up to 440, while far-camera encoder scores were 303–673 versus 820.

relationships.reason: Stitched scores fall well below E. R3L: Pong about 0 vs 21, Boxing 11–66 vs about 90, Breakout 14–71 vs 77–146. Some Breakout cells are barely above S. Abs (r26–r52).
relationships.display_finding: Stitched scores were approximately 0 versus 21 for Pong, 11–66 versus approximately 90 for Boxing, and 14–71 versus 77–146 for Breakout, sometimes barely exceeding the absolute-stitching baseline.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CarRacing standard, scrambled, and no-idle stitching conditions with green, red, or blue encoder variations
reader_labels.reason: R3L stitching scores are generally high and markedly exceed the absolute-stitching reference in these reported settings (r2–r4, r6–r10, r12–r16, r18–r19). The authors describe R3L as enabling zero-shot component reuse.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CarRacing slow-task and far-camera encoder conditions, and Atari stitching
reader_labels.reason: CarRacing slow-task and far-camera results are lower or variable, while the authors report a substantial performance drop for Atari stitching relative to end-to-end R3L; the Atari table also has large standard deviations (r5, r11, r17, r20–r25, r26–r52).
